text.3: CHAPTER 1 The Emperor's Last Mouthful I broke the first glass of that evening at exactly a quarter to eight, thir- ty seconds before I saw Nora Vance crossing the dance floor — which, now that I think about it, is pretty much everything you need to know about my relationship with luck. It was a champagne flute as thin as a diplomatic lie, and it slipped through my fingers just as the jazz band launched into some languid standard, somewhere beneath the heavy chandeliers of the ballroom. It shattered on the 1890 oak parquet with a crystalline sound, almost mu- sical — the kind of sound a sommelier would rather never hear outside a nightmare. A waiter in tails materialized from nowhere with a dust- pan, wearing that look that said, without a word: Mr. Rourke is once again contributing to the damage statistics. text.4: I'll tell you about Gus Thorne in a moment. For now it's enough to know that he was the kind of man who craved power the way others crave dessert, and that he had, on a mahogany side table beside the podi- um, a row of jars. Ten jars, like ten little altars. "The offerings," he called them. Every year, his former protégés scattered across the globe would send him, for his gala, a jar of the sauce that had made them famous — a kind of tribute, a kind of prayer. And Gus would taste them one by one, in front of everyone, and pronounce his verdicts. It was his favorite moment of the year. He liked to be fed by the hands of the people he'd brought to their knees. And that evening, among the hundred perfumed guests, was the woman who had broken my heart seven years earlier and who was, very soon, to set it beating again — though at the time I didn't know that, just as I didn't know that one of
text.5: "Like what?" She looked at me, and for a moment I had the strange feeling she wasn't looking me but me, at something about to happen at through that only she could already sense. "I don't know yet," she said. "But I won't like it." Up on the podium, Gus Thorne lifted the first little spoon over the first jar, the crowd fell silent with anticipatory pleasure, the saxophone died away, and the great empire of flavor entered, unknowing, its last three minutes of innocence. Let me step back a moment, though, because you can't understand a man's death without first understanding how badly someone, some- where, had earned the right to want it. Augustus Thorne was sixty-six and looked like a cardinal who'd dis- covered pleasure in place of faith. Broad shoulders wrapped in a be- spoke burgundy tuxedo, a silver mane combed straight back, big soft hands belonging to a man who had never scrubbed a
text.6: and then discarded. Ten of them, to be exact. Ten protégés, in ten cor- ners of the world. Ten people who had every reason to hate him — and who nonetheless, and this was the brilliant, grotesque part, sent him a jar of sauce every year, like vassals obliged to kiss their lord. I knew Gus better than I'd have liked. I'd written about him, drunk his wines, covered his galas. I'd watched him humiliate a seventy-year- old Vietnamese chef until the old man kissed his hand, trembling, to thank him for "the lesson." I'd seen him weep with emotion over a plate of pasta and then, that same evening, sign the ruin of the man who'd cooked it, because "talent without discipline is a crime." Gus wasn't evil in the dull way small men are evil. He was evil on a grand scale, with ap- petite, with relish, with the sincere conviction that the world owed him every mouthful he took from it. "Sometimes even people who don't deserve reading." I'd have had an answer for that. I still do, seven years later — a whole drawer of answers I never gave. I wanted to tell her it hadn't been my fault, which was a lie, or that it had been entirely my fault, which was an exaggeration she'd never have tolerated, because Nora can't stand flat- tery or martyrdom. So I said nothing, the way I usually do, and watched her watch the room — not as people, but as a platter of ingredients, each with its own smell, its rot or its freshness. text.8: Beside me, Nora tensed. I felt it in the air, like a change of pressure before a storm. She brought the vial of rose vinegar to her nose again. "Rourke," she whispered, without moving her lips. "What is it?" "Those jars." Her eyes slid across the row of ruby, green, and golden glass, as if counting souls. "Nine of them are old. I can smell it from here — oxidized sauce, lids sitting for months. They were sent long ago." "And the tenth?" She was silent a second too long. "The tenth," she said, "is fresh." Up under the chandelier, the Emperor of Flavor chose the first jar in the row, unscrewed the lid with a theatrical flourish, dipped his silver spoon, and carried it to his mouth, closing his eyes in pleasure before a room that held, as one man, its breath. ❧ 8
text.9: CHAPTER 2 The Poison in the Jar T he first jar wasn't the one that killed him. Nor the second. Gus Thorne tasted like a pianist warming up, eyes closed, pronounc- ing adjectives grand enough to ennoble a field marshal. "Romesco," he sighed at the first, smacking his tongue. "Pau, you volcanic boy — still too much vinegar. But I forgive you." Servile laugh- ter. "Ah, salsa verde. Bianca." A shadow crossed his face, too quick for everyone to catch. "Capers and memories." He moved from altar to altar, sipping, judging, and the crowd sipped along with him. Each verdict was a little spectacle of cruelty dressed up as affection. "Adjika! Tamara, my Abkhaz fire — still furious, still too salty, still in love with me, you can taste it in every fleck of pep- per." Laughter. "Nuoc cham. Minh. Perfect balance, as always. That boy could balance an earthquake. Pity perfection is so boring." Laughter.
